paragraphs.text: Mitchell-Riley syndrome is an autosomal recessive syndromic form of diabetes in which diabetes, usually beginning in the neonatal period, occurs with intestinal atresias (duodenal and/or jejunal atresia, with or without intestinal malrotation), gallbladder aplasia or hypoplasia, and hypoplastic or annular pancreas. Intrahepatic cholestasis and malabsorption that does not respond to pancreatic enzyme replacement are common, and many affected infants have died in the first year of life (Mitchell et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2010; Sansbury et al., 2015). Sansbury et al. (2015) reported affected individuals whose diabetes began in childhood rather than in the neonatal period.

paragraphs.text: Mitchell et al. (2004) described 5 infants (2 sib pairs from 2 families and 1 isolated case) with neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, jejunal atresia, duodenal atresia, and gallbladder aplasia or hypoplasia. One sib pair was born to consanguineous parents. Four of the children died in the first year of life despite aggressive medical management. One patient with a milder form survived without insulin. Pancreatic immunohistochemistry in 3 infants showed a few scattered chromogranin A-positive cell clusters but no insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin. Exocrine histology varied. In 1 patient from the consanguineous family, Mitchell et al. (2004) found no duplication or uniparental isodisomy of PLAGL1 at 6q24, no contiguous gene deletion involving the glucokinase gene, and no mutation in the coding sequence or splice sites of PDX1. They concluded that the disorder was probably a new autosomal recessive syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Chappell et al. (2008) reported a patient, born to consanguineous parents, with neonatal diabetes, intestinal atresias, and gallbladder agenesis. They noted that this was the first case with neonatal diabetes but no demonstrable structural abnormality of the pancreas, which indicated that a deficit in pancreatic function was involved. They suggested that cases with overlapping features such as malrotation, biliary atresia, and pancreatic hypoplasia, including those described by Martinez-Frias, might be variants of the same syndrome. Sequencing of KCNJ11, ABCC8, GCK, IPF1, HNF1B, NEUROD1, TCF7L2, and HNF6 found no mutations.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) reported 2 Turkish double first cousins (their fathers were brothers and their mothers sisters), with no history of parental consanguinity. Intestinal atresias were diagnosed at birth, but diabetes was not diagnosed until ages 3 and 6 years. The first patient, a girl born at 32 weeks' gestation weighing 1.65 kg, had duodenal atresia, a jejunal web, and Meckel diverticulum. Hyperglycemia was noted at age 2 years, and she presented with diabetic ketoacidosis at age 3 years. Insulin was below 2 microIU/ml, and anti-GAD, IAA, and ICA antibodies were negative. Small intestinal resection at age 5 years for recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding showed patches of gastric heterotopia. She had an absent gallbladder with an otherwise normal biliary tract, and her liver function tests had always been normal. Her identical twin had duodenal atresia and died at age 1 month of complications of prematurity and surgery. The second patient, a boy born at 34 weeks' gestation weighing 1.70 kg, had duodenal atresia and midgut malrotation. Diabetes was diagnosed at age 6 years, after asymptomatic fasting hyperglycemia had been found a year earlier. He also had chronic iron deficiency anemia of unknown cause, but no structural hepatobiliary abnormality. In both cousins, asymptomatic hyperglycemia lasted at least 1 year before diabetes was formally diagnosed. Both were alive at age 9 years. In a review of 8 previously reported molecularly confirmed cases, Sansbury et al. (2015) found duodenal atresia in all cases, gallbladder agenesis in 7 of 8, and intrahepatic cholestasis in 7 of 8 (ascites in another). Five of the 8 children had died, all within the first year of life.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) captured and deep-sequenced the exons in the shared homozygous regions from 1 proband (proband 2), the child of second cousins. The only nonsynonymous novel variant was a homozygous ser217-to-pro (S217P) change in the RFX6 gene. Sanger sequencing of all 19 RFX6 exons and splice junctions in 6 probands found mutations in 5. Probands 1, 4, and 5 died in the first few months of life. They were homozygous, respectively, for loss of the intron 2 splice donor site (IVS2+2T-C), an out-of-frame deletion in exon 7, and an arg181-to-gln (R181Q) substitution in the DNA-binding domain. Proband 3, alive at age 9 years and intermittently off insulin, was compound heterozygous for loss of the intron 6 donor site (IVS6+2T-G) and disruption of the intron 1 acceptor site (IVS1-12A-G). Proband 2, alive at age 4.5 years, was homozygous for S217P. All mutations were inherited from carrier parents. Functional studies showed that the IVS2+2T-C mutation abolished the normally spliced transcript in autopsy pancreas. R181Q completely abolished DNA binding, whereas S217P only modestly reduced it. No RFX6 mutation was found in the parents of a sixth proband, whom the authors considered most likely a phenocopy, or in a case of Martinez-Frias syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) generated Rfx6-null mice by replacing the first 5 exons, including the DNA-binding domain, with an eGFP-cre cassette. Homozygous mice were born at the expected mendelian ratio but fed poorly, had gross bowel distension due to small bowel obstruction, and died within 2 days of birth. Some had a smaller pancreas. At embryonic day 17.5, mutant pancreata contained many endocrine cells, but none expressed insulin, glucagon, somatostatin, or ghrelin. Pancreatic polypeptide-expressing cells were increased in number. Neurog3 expression was unaffected, whereas expression of downstream factors including Arx, Irx2, Pax6, Mafa, Neurod1, and Pdx1 was reduced. Rfx6 formed a heterodimeric DNA-binding complex with Rfx3, and the 2 factors cooperated in activating an X-box promoter.

(1992) described 2 sibs, born to consanguineous parents, with low birth weight, tracheoesophageal fistula, duodenal atresia, extrahepatic biliary atresia, hypoplastic pancreas, and hypospadias, and suggested a previously unreported autosomal recessive syndrome. Anneren et al. (1998) reported a lethal autosomal recessive syndrome of intrauterine growth retardation, intra- and extrahepatic biliary atresia, and esophageal and duodenal atresia. Gentile and Fiorente (1999) reported esophageal, duodenal, rectoanal, and biliary atresia, intestinal malrotation, malformed or hypoplastic pancreas, and hypospadias. Galan-Gomez et al. (2007) described a child of consanguineous parents with low birth weight, duodenal atresia, extrahepatic biliary atresia, hypoplastic pancreas, and intestinal malrotation, who died 60 days after birth with a normal 46,XX karyotype. They regarded this patient as confirming the autosomal recessive disorder described by Martinez-Frias et al. (1992). Smith et al. (2010) considered Mitchell-Riley syndrome distinct from Martinez-Frias syndrome (see NOMENCLATURE).

paragraphs.text: In 2 Turkish double first cousins with Mitchell-Riley syndrome and childhood-onset diabetes, Sansbury et al. (2015) found compound heterozygosity for a c.2596C-T transition in exon 18 of the RFX6 gene, resulting in an arg866-to-ter (R866X) substitution, and R726X. The mothers were heterozygous for R866X. Because R866X lies within 50 nucleotides of the last exon-exon boundary, it was predicted to escape nonsense-mediated decay and to produce a partially truncated protein with an intact DNA-binding domain. The authors proposed that this might explain the later onset of diabetes.

agent.process_note: I read the index and all 10 paper files: Smith et al. (2010) and Sansbury et al. (2015) in full, five abstracts, and two papers that have only their titles (Annerén 1998, Gentile 1999). I opened the start of TiGER (Liu 2008), a database paper Smith et al. used for expression data; it says nothing about the disorder, so I did not cite it. No HGNC reference data was supplied, so the intro gives no MIM number for RFX6, and the 6q21-q22 location comes from Smith et al. (2010). Three discrepancies stand. First, Sansbury's table gives the Martinovici patient's mutation as p.Arg181Gly, but Smith calls it R181Q. Second, the same table lists the two cousins as c.2176C>T homozygous, but the text says compound heterozygous. I followed the text. Third, Smith's main text says proband 2 was deep-sequenced, but their methods mention proband 1. I could not find the cDNA notation for Smith's variants in Smith; it is taken from Sansbury's table, which links each patient to a report.
